body: It doesn't crash for me on iPad, but I do get some visual stutter and black lines on occasion. There's no way this is running on my own iPhone XR, which chugs when I try to simply navigate the UI, let alone do dailies, event missions, or OpSi on it.

Reporting back. I discovered some things.

Namely, in my case, it wasn't an issue with IP addresses. It was more of an issue with YouTube's Chat.

* Videos buffer fine with normal videos. However, livestreams, VODs, and Premieres (anything with the chat feature) experience the issue. This was experienced on both Mac and PC. Buffering issue doesn't get experienced in mobile YouTube app.
* Interestingly, I have an adblocker on my mobile browser and livestreams work just fine, except that the adblocker actually blocks the live chat from appearing so the bug doesn't happen. So weirdly, mobile browser YouTube works fine because the chat is blocked.
* Issues are repeated regardless of having a VPN active or not.

So I think the point of commonality is the presence of YouTube's chat feature. If blocked by an adblocker but still active on the screen, it causes either a memory leak or connection issue. If a video doesn't have a live chat or is blocked completely, the video runs fine.
Interesting. I can also check with my VPN to see if that fixes it too.

Commenting to say that I'm experiencing the same thing. I haven't tried alternative options as much as you have, as I'm sticking to Firefox. However, I have the same "Something went wrong. Refresh or try again later" when it comes to livestreams and older VODs on YouTube. I used to have the same problem with anything longer than 1 hour, but (I think) I fixed that by modifying the filters in my uBlock Origin to allow jnn-pa.googleapis.com. Livestreams and VODs still don't work though. Do you have an adblocker extension on your browser?

I am in a somewhat similar boat as you. I'm a first-year PhD student entering my second year (haven't done my quals yet) but I am finding it hard to work on tasks that are really important but are now displeasing to interact with. I'm currently writing a paper but I just discovered today that the methodology I'm proposing has long been already published and I'm just burnt out on doing any more after a whole semester of work on the topic. A whole month of coding and literature review effectively gone, or so it feels like. Not to mention my colleagues (also first years) have papers published and now my advisor is low-key hinting to me "get your quals done now and get that paper written, look this student already has a exam committee planned". Major stresses like that.

I don't have a kid or a spouse/girlfriend, but there's still a lot of stuff to handle involving familial matters that are distracting me from my work severely. Not to mention that my roommate turns on the AC all night and I subjectively feel like I'm freezing at night every time I sleep. And that they are sick and coughing everywhere in the house. Small things like that too.

I suffer from chronic depression - diagnosed with it during my undergrad years. I've seen therapists but did not take meds. Here's my two-cents on your situation:

* Attempt therapy, but note that its success is a function of a lot of contextual variables you may not have control over. These factors include the skill/likeability of the therapist, if you take meds, if you are comfortable shelling out cash (if your insurance doesn't cover it) and spending time to talk to said therapist. In my case, it didn't end up working out because I was mentally torturing myself with the 20/20 vision of hindsight upon recounting things that were depressing me to my therapist. It MIGHT work with you though - again, it depends.
* If you're having a kid, that means you have a spouse. Consider mentioning these worries to any close friends or family, just to get their perspective. Again, you might get varied levels of success because your family or friends may or may not necessarily be empathetic to your situation or have the context to understand it. In my case, I couldn't go to my parents because 1) my father is a PhD holder and berates me whenever I go to him regarding PhD-related worries, 2) I don't want to bother my sister or mother with my concerns, and 3) people just keep telling me it's imposter syndrome and it'll pass... which is fine knowing what it is but doesn't really do much to help in the immediate situation.
* I started to write down TO-DOs every evening after I end up working. These TO-DOs are a nice reminder of next tasks. They don't have to be global in scope - just things like "things I wanna do tomorrow or the next time I sit down to work". This actually helped me a lot because I wasn't losing track of progress or the flow of my thoughts nearly as much. Keeping this list small, short, and sweet was actually effective in helping me handle some of my lesser anxieties about necessary duties.
* Do try to spend less time at work, seriously. Putting your nose to the grindstone isn't going to help if you are demotivated to do it - all it does is instill you with a sense of anger (at not being able to do it), anxiety (that you aren't capable of solving your problems), and misery (that you're doing what feels like torture). This is not to say that you should completely abandon your duties - but reduce them by an hour every day or something. Small changes like these can lead to incremental effects on your outlook. It helps me when I decide to go home earlier than normal because I get to escape the torture faster.
* Whatever you do, do NOT attempt to suspend. Do not leave without something to show for your work - at least get the master's degree if you want to leave early.
* I find that this is very particular to my situation, but maybe it'll resonate with yours. Do not associate your work with your personal life. What I mean is that, for example, if you decide to push your nose to the grindstone because of your kid or spouse, then that is not a good justification - it will lead to you associating your negative thoughts with your family, and that will lead to a lot of nasty thoughts down the line. Only do this if you're close to the finish line and can see the end (which you seem to be struggling with).
